utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, good morning, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce Raluca Dragan from Romania who is one of our legal interns who will be helping us today during this session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Buna dimineata." Good morning, Mr. Tieger. Good morning, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. We received the report contained in your periodic disclosure report. I'd like to ask you whether you have anything to add to the report we received?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I got the impression that you wanted to hear more details on how we missed the items that were the subject of the two recent disclosure violation motions and I am actually prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. But, Your Honour, at the outset I have to say that when the Prosecution team detects an error of -- in its disclosure, it's never routine to us. And on the contrary, the team members involved in search and disclosure matters - and there are many - they are very upset about it, including myself. And then we immediately establish why these items have been missed and try to find a way to systematically and comprehensively react to this. In relation to these three Bosnian statements we missed, we found that they came from the files that we received from the Bosnian authorities many years ago, and these files were usually quite big and contained a considerable amount of statements, mostly inculpatory statements related to a given crime. The statements were missed in the initial search and all subsequent searches because of the same OCR problem. And as these three statements were never translated and also never separately processed into the OTP databases, the counter measures for possible OCR problems never found them either. Fortunately, the lawyer preparing for the cross-examination of a Defence witness looked into this file as this Defence witness was implicated in certain crimes, and only then found the statements and we immediately disclosed it. And as we have seen from the disclosure report, we immediately have reacted to it and we have meanwhile disclosed rules of the road files already in a great extent and we are still doing it, but before doing so we have to remove internal work products from these files, and, therefore, we will need about two more weeks to complete the entire disclosure of the rules of the road files related to the crimes charged in this case here. And just if you want to know more of the rules of the road files, I also have to tell you that very many of these files are duplicates or triplicates or even more. As an example, when ten persons are implicated in a given crime, you have ten very similar files because for each perpetrator the Bosnian authorities compare a separate file. And the Defence is also aware already of such files and has received quite a number of them because they showed up in the spreadsheets that we have compiled for the 66(B) requests for the Defence. That's the first group of missed items. And the second one is a report for Witness Vasiljevic, and I must say that troubled me the most because I was personally involved in this interview and it occurred at a time not long before the disclosure dead-line for witness statements of the Trial Chamber. The OTP has established procedures how to deal with such information reports. The investigators conducting the interview have to prepare the report. They then have to process it into the OTP evidence collection. They get ERN'd and then disclosed. That is standard procedure, and we have described this procedure in more details in appendix B to the disclosure report of the 28th of July, 2011, where Mr. Hogan, investigator, has described it in all steps. When disclosure is particularly urgent, for instance, when we have to meet a disclosure dead-line or when there is a witness upcoming, sometimes the disclosure is done informally, also via e-mail, before a given document is ERN'd. In this particular case, the information report was prepared in time but unfortunately it was not processed into the OTP evidence collection but remained in the personal electronic file of the investigator. I, myself, was convinced that it was disclosed because of the standard procedure. Only when I prepared for the cross-examination of Mr. -- of General Vasiljevic, I realised that the information report was not showing in the spreadsheet for this witness that we had prepared according to the 66(B) request. At that time I still thought that this disclosure report -- sorry, that this information report was disclosed and I thought probably, because of the urgency according to -- via e-mail without ERN-ing. You can see that easily from my disclosure letter that was attached to the 78th disclosure violation motion because you can see an additional remark reflecting my thinking in this letter. However, the review -- the internal review did not show any trace of any disclosure. As a consequence of the circumstance in this particular case, the team lawyers and investigators have been directed to review their personal electronic folders so that the Prosecution can exclude any similar human error in the future. We also have requested the files of the lawyers and investigators who have meanwhile left our team and left the OTP, that they be retrieved from the archives and we will also review these files. It will take us about two weeks to do all this. That is what I can say in relation to the two disclosure violations at issue in your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Do you wish to make any observations, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much. First of all, we want to thank the Chamber for the efforts that it's been making on our behalf, both yesterday in connection with our request for the United Kingdom's documents and today by asking the Prosecution to provide an oral explanation for the disclosure violations. And we thank Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff for her detailed explanation of those. I'd like to just give you some additional information on each violation, the first one being the 77th disclosure violation motion, where the Prosecution reported that the optical character recognition technology hadn't recognised the names. In the Prosecution's consolidated response to the accused's third, fourth, and fifth motions for a finding of disclosure violations and for remedial measures on the 6th of July, 2010, some two and a half years ago, the Prosecution said that they were already searching for the optical character recognition text of image files and that these multiple layers of searches enable the Prosecution to locate all witness-related materials. They went on to say that they'd implemented an additional measure of searching through PDF and Microsoft Office files so that they could also, through optical character recognition and other technology, do a full text search of those documents. In the Prosecution submission of a report concerning additional measures related to Rule 66(A) disclosure filed on the 20th of August, 2010, the Prosecution reported that this search had been completed for all witnesses. In its notice of compliance with the Trial Chamber's further decision on the 1st of December, 2010, the Prosecution further reported that all four additional measures are complete and all statements of their witnesses have been disclosed as of the 30th of November, 2010. In the Prosecution's response to Dr. Karadzic's 33rd, 34th, 35th, and 37th motion for disclosure violations on the 4th of February, 2011, it was said that the Prosecution conceded that it had violated Rule 66(A)(ii). And although the concrete measures implemented by the Prosecution at the Trial Chamber's request had been somewhat effective, by virtue of human error the statements at issue had been missed because the witness's name in the statement was not recognised by the optical character recognition process relied upon by the Prosecution. And the Prosecution promised to continue to re-review the documents and the disclosure logs to identify any material which had been omitted from disclosure. In the Prosecution's disclosure report of the 27th of July, 2011, the Prosecution identified technical limitations in searching documents with poor quality as one of the reasons for the previous disclosure violations and it detailed the steps in which it was taking to remedy that situation, including assigning Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff to personally manage all aspects of this disclosure. And it assured the Chamber that the Prosecution has taken steps to ensure that all relevant interviews had been reviewed and disclosed when required. In the Prosecution's response to the 74th motion for finding of disclosure violation on the 29th of October, 2012, the Prosecution explained that its failure to disclose two documents from Defence Witness Andrej Demurenko was because during the electronic search carried out for Witness Demurenko, the optical character recognition technology did not recognise the documents containing Colonel Demurenko's name or signature. So I think that nothing we've heard today can give us any confidence that the violations due to the optical character recognition problems will be eradicated. With respect to the 78th disclosure violation motion, the Prosecution has explained that the statement was not entered into the OTP evidence collection. In its Prosecution's response to the accused's sixth motion for finding of disclosure violation and for remedial measures on the 12th of July, 2010, some two and a half years ago, the Prosecution acknowledged that the failure to disclose two proofing notes for Prosecution witnesses had been through oversight and indicated that the Prosecution has assigned a person to supplement the existing inter-case communication regarding witness disclosure by following up regarding the production of proofing notes, including their prompt assignment of evidence reference numbers. It reported in its Prosecution's submission of report concerning additional measures on the 20th of August, 2010, that that measure had been completed. In the Prosecution's response to Dr. Karadzic's 48th motion for finding of disclosure violation and sanctions on the 16th of May, 2011, the Prosecution said that the three interview reports that it had missed had been located within the internal computer network of the Prosecution and had been overlooked. And they realised that they needed to search certain secure drives in their network. In the Prosecution's 49th motion for finding of disclosure violation on the 8th of June, on their response on the 8th of June, 2011, the Prosecution explained how it missed the transcript of the interview with General Vlado Lizdek because it had not properly been entered into the Prosecution's evidence unit when it was received. The Prosecution reported that in light of the oversight it had identified interviews at a category of documents that should be further examined and isolated interviews and undertook a systematic review of the material to try to remedy the disclosure violations. In the Prosecution's response to the 56th motion for finding of disclosure violations on the 18th of August, 2011, the Prosecution explained that the proofing note that it had not disclosed of the witness had been -- had not been recorded in the disclosure log by another trial team and had therefore not been discovered and disclosed. In the Prosecution's response to the 58th motion for finding of disclosure violation, on the 7th of the September, 2011, the Prosecution explained that a transcript of witness testimony in another ICTY case had not been discovered because of human error. This was not the first disclosure violation with respect to General Vasiljevic. In the Prosecution's response to Dr. Karadzic's 71st motion for disclosure violation on 15 May 2012, the Prosecution conceded that it failed to timely disclose a 2005 information report of an interview with General Vasiljevic, and the only explanation was that their previous searches had not located this material and that it had been discovered by another trial team within the Office of the Prosecutor. So I think nothing that we've heard today can give us confidence that the violations due to materials not being entered into the Prosecution's database, can be eradicated. To put these latest violations in context, the Prosecution has failed to disclose 411 statements of its own witnesses which have been in its possession since before May 2009 when that dead-line had expired. Since the commencement of the trial, the Prosecution has disclosed 342.272 pages of exculpatory material, the vast majority of which was not disclosed as soon as practicable and which was in its various collections before the trial had commenced. On 62 occasions during the course of this trial, the Trial Chamber has made an express finding that the Prosecution had violated its disclosure obligations. The violations have continued and will continue, and as long as the violations will continue we will continue to make a record of those violations. And the violations will appear likely to continue throughout the trial, your deliberations, before the Appeals Chamber if there's a conviction, and the review process if a conviction is re -- affirmed on appeal. We welcome the Prosecution's initiative to disclose its collection of witness statements known as the rules of the road collection, and we see this as a very positive first step. The Prosecution has disclosed to us on Friday 1474 items totalling 267.343 pages, which it indicates is in the B/C/S language, majority of interviews conducted by authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina after -- during and after the war. We see open-file disclosure as the best solution to these disclosure violations. Give us the documents and the time and resources to review them and we'll have no grounds to complain about withheld disclosure, and there'll be no more disclosure violations and no more disclosure violation motions. And with the greatest respect, we believe that the Trial Chamber has capitulated too readily to the obstacles to open-file disclosure thrown up by the Prosecution. Sensitive material can be segregated by the Prosecution, can be excluded from the access given to the Defence team, and can be reviewed by the Chamber or an independent party acting at its direction. After all these disclosure violations, requiring the Prosecution to segregate those items is a modest burden to ensure that it finally complies with its disclosure obligations. Thank you for your time and attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you wish to add anything, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but only very briefly. I mean, I agree with Mr. Robinson when he points out all the previous violations and he has identified the filings and the motions and the motion responses related to this. And in the disclosure report that we filed on Friday, we have actually listed the -- in paragraphs 5 to 9 and also in paragraph -- in footnote 3 all the major filings that show the measures taken when a certain disclosure violation was found. We have -- and all these measures that have been taken - and Mr. Robinson has actually referred to them - have one thing in common, that is that every time we tried to solve the situation comprehensively and systematically and we added layer of layer of searches to find these things and we did find a lot of measures -- a lot of items with these additional measures. And I have explained to you why in the case of the -- of the three statements for Mr. Bazdar and the protected witness, why all these layers still missed the items, and, that is, a text search was not successful because we never had a translation and we never had a proper index for the particular statements in the system. So the text searches pick up on names when there is a name as a text in our system, but it wasn't for these three. And I've explained why that is so. And in relation to the report for Witness Vasiljevic, we have -- we have done all these searches and the additional measures and the additional layers, but what we had not included and we had not envisioned because it should not be possible, that an information report remains on a personal file of an investigator and that is now what we are doing now. We are searching now the personal files of persons in the Prosecution team, current ones and even previous ones, that have ever dealt with witnesses. And that was something that we hadn't foreseen and that is yet another additional layer. So the measures that we took didn't fail. The only thing is we haven't thought of this particular possibility because we thought it would not happen because we have a standard procedure for doing the work with witnesses. And in relation to the request of an open file, I mean we have already litigated that in writing and I don't want to add to this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The booths have not been given the text read by Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff and Mr. Robinson. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, I appreciate the hard work by the interpreters, appreciate it very much. Speaking for myself, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I'm of the opinion that at the bottom of the circumstances lies the fact that the Prosecution itself does not know what is contained in its very own evidence collection. Is my observation correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me tell you, we are talking about 10 million of pages. That's the extent of the evidence collection. And of course nobody in this team or in any other team knows all these 10 million pages. That's why we have to rely on searches, electronic searches, and these electronic searches should pick up all relevant materials. We, of course, know our witnesses and we also now get a lot of information on the Defence witnesses, but we definitely do not know the content of the 10 million pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To put it directly, do you foresee that further disclosure violations are unavoidable despite the measures put in place?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no guarantee that we will not have any disclosure violations in the future. There is no guarantee to this, because human error is very -- cannot be excluded and our search layers, as you have seen now, although we added so many, they still, for particular reasons, miss a certain item. I think we would not be honest to say we can guarantee there will be no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your submissions and we'll leave the matter at that. There's another few matters I'd like to deal with. Yes, Mr. Tieger, the Chamber received a complaint from Witness Milan Martic regarding the decision of the Registry denying the request to assign Defence counsel. So I wonder whether, if you would like to respond to that complaint; and if yes, I would like to have it by the close of business tomorrow, Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President. I haven't -- am aware of it generally but haven't seen it. I think the likelihood of our responding is low, but it's prudent to look at it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber received the courtesy copy and I was told that it was not officially filed yet. Probably you will get it. Next, Mr. Robinson probably. The Chamber received the Defence motion for subpoena General Zdravko Tolimir, which was filed 12th of March, 2013. I wonder whether it's clear that -- from the motion if the Defence has exhausted its endeavour to secure the voluntary co-operation from the witness in that the last e-mail correspondence from Mr. Gajic only seems to indicate that he prefers that nothing be planned early March as he has a dead-line for the submission of a notice of appeal. So if you could take a look into the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I can advise you right now because when I received that e-mail I told Professor Gajic to --if he would please speak with General Tolimir, and if General Tolimir wanted to testify, to let us know by the 7th of March, otherwise we would assume that he didn't want to testify. And as you can see from my e-mail to him, he never heard anything from him, and to this day we haven't heard anything from him. So I think the best thing to do is to have a response from General Tolimir to our motion. And if there's any hint that he's willing to testify, we could pursue it. But from every piece of information we have including his conversations with Dr. Karadzic and my conversations with his legal advisor, we have no expectation whatsoever that he's willing to testify in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I wonder whether you would like to contact Mr. Gajic one last time and then whether his notice of appeal has been filed and then it's clear that the general does not want to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, I have to make this observation, having observed evidence of Defence witnesses so far. In earlier phases of the case and during the Rule 98 bis submissions, the accused made it clear that he would challenge all the charges in the indictment, including the occurrence of crimes. However, the Chamber has noticed that recently, especially in relation to the Srebrenica component, the accused has called witnesses who themselves have testified to the occurrence of crimes, thus triggering the Chamber to form an impression that his defence is, as a result, focusing more on his alleged responsibility for or linkage to the crimes charged. More specifically, the Chamber is wondering if Mr. Karadzic is conceding that certain crimes occurred. If that is the case, the Chamber would appreciate if the accused or Mr. Robinson could liaise with the Prosecution on certain agreed facts and come back to the Chamber with the result of discussions. This would be an exercise not only saving a great amount of time but also allowing the Chamber and the parties to focus on more important issues. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could just raise one quick matter in connection with the Tolimir subpoena and, more broadly, with respect to similarly situated witnesses who may arise, and that is the following -- oh, and I should add this is a matter we've discussed with Mr. Robinson in anticipation of this possibility. Obviously, the Prosecution is in no position to meaningfully prepare for cross-examination of such witnesses and even beyond that there's no guarantee that these witnesses will even testify at all, and under their particular circumstances may refuse. And they, as the Court recognises, are witnesses whose preparation would involve extremely substantial efforts because of the nature of the witness and his involvement in the events. So to avoid a lavish waste of resources expended in preparation for matters that do not arise for one of the two reasons I raised, we agreed with Mr. Robinson - but of course it's up to the Chamber - that the cross-examination of witnesses such as those would be deferred for two weeks after the examination-in-chief, which would actually be half of the time we would normally expect if we got a meaningful 65 ter summary or a statement in advance, but at least compromises the circumstances enough to take into account what would otherwise be a very unfortunate wasteful expenditure of Prosecution resources and I presume Chamber resources as well. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have some situations such as with General Krstic. We were unable to meet with the witness before the witness's testimony because they refuse, and we don't know until they come in to take the oath whether or not they're going to give testimony. So we think it's reasonable for the Prosecution not to have to prepare for that eventuality immediately. And so if, in fact, the witness testifies, which we hope they will, then we think it is reasonable that the Prosecution be given some period of time after the direct examination to prepare for and then conduct their cross-examination. But that's completely up to you, but that's how we see it anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, it's difficult to issue its guidance in vacuum at the moment. All I can say is to see how it evolves, and, as one Judge says, we play it by ear. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the problem, Mr. President. If we're simply playing it by ear, then the Prosecution -- the decision is actually made. The attorney handling that witness will have to prepare even if the Court later decides, well, that was unnecessary and unfair given the circumstances. That's why we're seeking some assurance from the Court that there will be a deferral of the cross-examination under such circumstances. Otherwise, we have no choice but to go ahead and prepare, thereby implicating the very concerns I expressed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us take General Krstic. Defence is in the position -- I'm sorry. The Defence is not in the position to know what Krstic is going to testify; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, no, that's not exactly correct, Mr. President, because we have his previous testimony in his own trial as well as statement he's given to the Office of the Prosecutor as well as our own factual investigation, so we have some reasonable expectation as to what he would testify to if he testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, the Prosecution is in the same position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So why Prosecution does need more time to prepare its cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Because the Rules provide for that, Mr. President. This is completely different situation. It is their witness. They can attempt to elicit from him what they choose, but the Rules provide for the Prosecution to be noticed with the facts upon which the witness will testify so that we can undertake adequate cross-examination preparation in the effort to illuminate the truth. I mean, this is a quite different situation, it seems to me, when the one party calls a witness from whom it attempts -- it hopes to elicit favourable information to its case and the other party has to, in advance, adhere itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, my question is all the material the Defence has in its custody are -- have been disclosed to the Prosecution, haven't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President, we're talking about two different situations. Let me go back to the situation I talked about earlier and I think they would involve potentially different solutions. And I began with the case of Mr. Tolimir. What you're asking is to have the Prosecution - which, by the way, is working very, very long hours already, as I know the Defence is - to invest a great deal of time into the preparation for cross-examination of a witness who may not testify at all, and who, if he does testify, may only testify to a very, very narrow portion of events. Now, that strikes me as a very unfair and unnecessary expenditure of Prosecution resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I see your point. But let's go back to General Krstic; why you need extra time after his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It may not be the case, but it cannot -- I mean, it's not fair to analogise precisely to the situation of the Defence. The reason -- I mean, you could -- you could, I think, essentially scrap 65 ter (G) under the rationale that the Prosecution essentially can find itself in essentially the same position as the Defence. The Rules provide for notice of what -- and this implicates the litigation we've been involved in concerning the provision of adequate 65 ter summaries and now the proposal that the -- this intractable problem be resolved by the provision in advance of statements. The fact is that for reasons that we've come to appreciate during the course -- that all of us I think have come to appreciate during the course of this case and other cases, meaningful cross-examination requires meaningful notice so that the cross-examination preparation can be focused. The Rules provide for that, and that's all we're seeking. Now, it may well be the case that -- and I understand this part of the Court's position - that sometimes the nature of the witness, the nature of his -- of that witness's testimony can mean that the length of time after the examination-in-chief for the Prosecution to fairly be asked to commence its cross-examination may vary. And we were, in the case of Mr. Krstic, prepared to begin on relatively short notice under that situation and we prepared to do so. But, as I think the Court is now aware, that's a different situation from the situation of witnesses like Mr. Tolimir. Nevertheless, the -- if it's true that in some circumstances it may be possible for the Prosecution to commence cross-examination right away based on its general preparations for that witness, it is certainly also true that on other occasions and perhaps many occasions fairness will demand that there be a deferral of time before cross-examination commences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- speaking for myself here, I think the point is that why should a party have to spin its wheels for something that might not happen, given the scope of this case and the intensity of the pace of the case, that's -- to me is the point because we all have many, many tasks to do. This situation could well be reversed and that's why I'm helping Mr. Tieger here because it's an issue of the parties, and maybe the Chamber doesn't have the same problems that we do, but we don't have time to prepare for witnesses who aren't going to testify - that's the bottom line - and I'm sure the Prosecution doesn't either, so why make them? That's how we see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I believe the Chamber has never denied a remedy which is, in fact, sound and warranted. I'll discuss with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Maric. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask you to make pauses between questions and answers and also to speak slowly so that everything would be recorded. Dr. Maric, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't give any statement?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, on arriving here on Saturday, I gave a statement on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D7931 is the document that I would ask to be shown in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document has not been released, Mr. Karadzic, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As you know, the e-court system was down this weekend. We've had this document sent to the people who are releasing them on behalf of the Registry, and apparently they haven't done that yet. So I'm not sure if we can print out a copy of the statement and give it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: To the statement, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed with the hard copies that we have. Probably the witness has his hard copy as well, otherwise we can print it and provide him with the statement. Do you have your statement with you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while this is being printed, I would ask the following: Could the Chamber encourage the Registry to enable me to upload from my room documents in the system? I can do that during the night and then they would be released by the case manager. Otherwise, sometimes we really have a problem. There is a bottleneck with the uploading system and working with any electronical equipment is really at 19th century level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This seems to go beyond by purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, one thing that is within your purview is the inequality of arms that we suffer as a result of the e-court system because the Prosecution can upload documents directly into e-court, Mr. Reid can do that; but for the Defence, apparently, they don't trust us, so they put another layer. So the ITSS people from the Registry are the ones who only can upload Defence documents. utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should now like to read the summary of the statement of Dr. Veljko Maric in English. [In English] Dr. Veljko Maric was a surgeon in the Foca hospital. The hospital near Foca was the only hospital in the municipality, although there were outpatient clinics in other towns. Before the war, the hospital was run by republican organs which paid the salaries, provided everyday materials and human resources. After the beginning of the conflict the organising body changed from BH to the Republika Srpska. Before the war, the hospital kept 30 to 90 days' worth of medical supplies; however, after the conflict started the stocks of medicines were used, and as the original government organs were no longer functioning the supplies were not replenished. Therefore, medicine was provided by humanitarian organisations and all the medicine was efficiently used. Despite this, there were shortages of medical supplies throughout the war. The ethnic structure of the hospital staff was mixed until July 1992, when Muslim employees left the hospital. These employees left of their own free will, they were not driven out. Veljko Maric estimates that the hospital was running on full capacity throughout the war. There was no theft of medical supplies from Foca hospital and the building suffered some damages from the fighting which was not able to be repaired, but this only slightly affected the hospital's functioning. It was difficult for patients and staff to visit the hospital, as access to the hospital was blocked by the Green Berets who would not let Serbs pass through the barricade particularly in the first few days of the fighting. Only the wounded were allowed to pass through. On 8th of April, 1992, the Green Berets stopped the bus and transported the staff to the hospital -- that transported the staff to the hospital and would not let it pass; therefore, the staff had to continue to the hospital on foot. Many patients of different ethnicities asked to be transferred to areas where their ethnicity was in a majority and efforts were taken to accommodate all of those requests. In 1992, the hospital staff attempted to hand-over the sick children of other ethnic groups to the Muslim authorities for their own safety; however, the Muslim authorities refused to take them. The KPD received a separate supply of medicine from the Red Cross and on a number of occasions the hospital had to borrow supplies from the KPD as theirs had run out. Foca hospital also assisted with medical supplies for the KPD and prisoners would be treated at the hospital on a regular basis. Further, the doctors from Foca hospital would treat the prisoners at the KPD when the doctors from the KPD left. They provided assistance whenever it was required, usually on a daily basis. There was no relationship with the military or civilian authorities and these organisations could not influence the work of the doctors. The provision of medical help was not affected by religions, ethnic affiliation, or skin colour. Everyone who entered the hospital received treatment; no discrimination was made. As far as Dr. Veljko Maric is aware, no doctors in the Foca hospital discriminated on the grounds of religion or ethnicity. In the first few days of the fighting, the hospital also took in civilians who had nowhere else to go. Both Serb and Muslim civilians stayed and received the food. [Interpretation] That is the short summary.

All of them continued with their treatment until they were cured and released from the hospital, specifically in this case from the paediatric ward. In April 1992 we admitted patients on a daily basis from Foca, Visegrad, Cajnice, Rogatica, and Gorazde. In the month of April we admitted 149 patients with different conditions of Muslim ethnicity. Thus, in May, June, July, August, and September we admitted patients, and in that period we had 268 Muslim patients beginning with pregnant women, adults, and children who sought our help. They were treated and discharged throughout 1992.

Patients had a choice to go outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina towards Uzice or Pljevlja, in Montenegro, or Sokolac or Sarajevo, but they came to Foca because regionally they belonged to us, they were our patients, and probably they trusted us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, on the 16th, Saturday, we provided notice that we were going to be using this document, and I believe - and I'm looking at the e-mail but I might be wrong about this - but in the e-mail of the 16th which was sent to the Prosecution, one of the documents that was attached to that e-mail was this document, 1D7933, which bears the ERN 0039-1549. So I don't understand why Mr. Zec hasn't received it on Saturday with the e-mail that was sent to his team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the e-mail again. I don't see it. I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if you wouldn't mind, if Mr. Zec can just walk over here I'll show it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that it is just a one-page document, shall we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the circumstances, the Chamber will allow the accused to use the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it in e-court? All right. We're going to use the ELMO then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, can you tell us whether Dr. Asim Prutina is someone you know. Is the name familiar?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my colleague. He's an internist and he's the director of the medical centre in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you read the heading here and can you tell the Trial Chamber where Pljevlja is?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: This is a list of wounded and ill patients who were sent to the hospital in Pljevlja. Pljevlja is a town 100 kilometres away from Gorazde in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Vulnus sclopetarium and others. Can you tell us what kind of injury that is that is recorded on this page?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: These are injuries due to fire-arms, all of them. All of them, actually. I don't see any explosives or anything like that, so different body parts were wounded by fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the names of the patients, do they indicate any ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: It's mixed, which would correspond to the population of Gorazde, different ethnic backgrounds, Serbs, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha. Carapic is the last name under 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Karadzic will do that, but when he said there is a mix of ethnicity can we know exactly what -- where he is referring to and what ethnicity these people are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's Doctor's answer was mixed. Probably he was about to read through. Could you be more specific when you said it's mixed, Dr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both ethnicities are there. On this list of ten patients, there are two Carapic's who are Serbs and there are eight Muslims who were sent to the hospital in Pljevlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Carapics are under which number?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Seven and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page now. That's number 11. Can you tell us who this is and can you tell us why this person was sent to Pljevlja?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: This is an injury of the spine, again due to a fire-arm. It is Salaka Jusuf, a Muslim, who is being sent to Pljevlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page now. Please, again, the heading, and can you tell us where Uzice is?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: This is a list of persons who were wounded in Gorazde and they were sent from Gorazde about 100 or 200 kilometres -- no, about 130 kilometres away, that's where Uzice is. That's a town in Serbia. The patients were sent from Gorazde due to their injuries. Again they're due to fire-arms, all the injuries registered here. Except Radovic Dragoljub, the remaining nine persons are of Muslim ethnicity, whereas Radovic Dragoljub is an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the date of admission?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: The 4th of May, the 8th of June; that is to say, from the 4th until the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page now. Can you just cast a glance. Similar, but the first one, Goran, is a Serb and all the rest are Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page now. Also all of them are Muslims and Prutina signed this and that's the end of May; right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how would you assess these wounds? Most of them are sclopetarium; right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sclopetarium, could you please explain to the participants what that means?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: That's an exit/entry wound due to fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the next page, please. Thank you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, again it says wounded persons. Where is this Sokolac, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Sokolac is a hospital which is about 80 or 90 kilometres away from Gorazde. It's in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, Republika Srpska. And two patients, on the 6th and 7th of May, were sent from Gorazde to the hospital in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under whose control was Sokolac then?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Serbs controlled Sokolac, and the hospital was managed and headed by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last page, please. Can you tell us where these persons were sent and what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: These were patients who came to the hospital in Foca, surgery, where I work and they came on these dates here when they were sent because they had been injured. They had surgery, they were treated, and some of them like number 3, Prsusa [phoen] Jusuf, due to longer medical treatment I transferred him to Sarajevo, to Sarajevo in Kosevo, because of the chest wounds that he had sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Prutina, Dr. Prutina, did he know who was working in Foca and who he was sending patients to?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Of course. We are friends and colleagues and we just parted briefly during the war. We're friends to this day. We visit each other. We knew who does what and who was performing surgery because this is a joint medical institution. It used to be an SOUR in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last page, please. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber where Dr. Prutina sent these two patients, laceral contusion and the other one is explosives, so it's a laceration and a wound due to explosive.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were sent to Belgrade 300 kilometres away. That's what my colleague did. Since they had to be treated for a long time, he thought that he should not send them to us because we were a smaller institution. He immediately wanted to send them to a major medical centre and that is why he decided, that is why my colleague decided, to send them to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted and, actually, half of it is in Latin and the rest are names. So the only thing that has to be translated are the headings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3132, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for Dr. Maric at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Karadzic. Dr. Maric, as you have noted except for these four documents that we admitted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. After a break we are going to take for 15 minutes, you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Zec. 15 minutes. We'll resume at quarter past 11.00. --- Break taken at 11.01 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would only note that the previous document that was discussed was, in fact, sent to the Prosecution as Mr. Robinson suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let me ask you first a couple of background questions. You are member of the SNSD party, that is Alliance of Independent Social Democrats of Milorad Dodik, are you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am also a deputy in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you moved to the SNSD party, you were member of the SDS party; this is correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No. I was just a deputy after the first democratic elections. My term of office was in 1997, and I was a deputy on behalf of the Serbian Democratic Party and I served my duty for four years then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 24 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, excuse me, Mr. Zec. Mr. President, because of the ongoing technical difficulties, the Prosecution exhibits aren't available to Dr. Karadzic other than being printed out in hard copy. So I'm sorry to bother you with this. We could ask somebody to be doing that right now, but could we perhaps take another short recess so that he could have access to the exhibits that the Prosecution is going to be using.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say something about the transcript. Dr. Maric said that as a representative of the Serbian Democratic Party as a movement at that time. So he was not necessarily a member. He was a representative on behalf of the Serbian Democratic Party as a movement, and this part "as a movement" has not been recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How many documents are you going to use in your cross-examination, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Not that many, Mr. President. But I just don't know how we can work without e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I understand the situation, it's roughly as follows: The documents that are not available in e-court are documents that were not previously in the system. In addition, Mr. Reid has worked out a system which allows those documents to be shown on Sanction and has e-mailed to the Defence hard copies of those particular documents. The problem is that while Mr. Robinson has those documents because of the e-mail system, I understand that Mr. Karadzic does not have access to e-mail from where he's sitting, so he can't simply click on those documents and see them, so, and -- which is why, I understand, he's asking for the hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we adjourn and resume at 11.30, would it be sufficient, about eight minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think so. There's 15 documents to be printed out. I think it can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this portal should stop being the portal of the accused, it should become the portal of the Defence so that I could use it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that it is now -- they are now available in the e-court. Then we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I asked that 65 ter 24730 be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is, Dr. Maric, a publication of the SDS party for Serbian lands entitled programme. Can we have next page in B/C/S. Dr. Maric, can you confirm that we see here Srbinje. Can you confirm that Srbinje was the new name of Foca after the Bosnian Serb authorities renamed the town?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you confirm under item number 1 it is your name?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will tender this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a list of candidates for the elections in 1997. This is the election list for the local elections, the first democratic ones held in 1997 where I'm shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are tendering the first page and this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And there is one more page. The list goes on to the next page. In total three pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Maric, the accused in this case either privately or professionally?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: I do, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: How exactly?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic is the president of Republika Srpska. He was the first president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you knew him -- so, for example, did you meet him during the war personally?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew who Dr. Karadzic was as he's a psychiatrist. I had an occasion during the times of the former Yugoslavia to meet him at some lectures and meetings of doctors, doctors from the former Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And only quick yes or no answer. During the war, did you have an opportunity to meet him personally?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Would you remember the date, occasion?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: The president of the republic visited the health institution, that is to say the hospital, in Foca and that was the first time I met the president during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us in paragraph 5 of your statement that the conflicts which spread across Bosnia and Herzegovina forced people to go where their own people were. Dr. Maric, by the end of 1992, there were almost no non-Serbs living in Foca; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No. Foca is a town which had a population of approximately 50 per cent Serbs and 50 per cent Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Petko Cancar from Foca told the RS Assembly and the accused on 2nd April 1993 that only one people lives on the territory of Foca and there's only one religion practiced there. This was the reality of Foca in 1993, Dr. Maric, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: In 1993 that was during the war, rather than before the war; that is, during the war. But you have seen that I mentioned that life was not -- I had 260, I wanted patients at the hospital. How many there were in the town, this I don't know. 268 non-Serb patients are those that I had at the hospital, so certainly their families were there as well, but I don't know how many people that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I refer to P01367, English page 25, B/C/S e-court page 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In May 1993 at the 30th Assembly, Petko Cancar said: "I cannot persuade the international community, but I can persuade you that there is currently not a single Muslim in the area of the largest municipality in the former BH." Again, Dr. Maric, this was the reality of Foca in 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Well, let me not repeat once again, as I don't know this. I'm not familiar with Petko Cancar's statements and I cannot interpret them. But I started from the point of view of my work. That was the number of patients I had, so on the basis of that I can judge how many families were there as well because probably the patients were not there alone with other families.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I referred to P01371, English page 78, B/C/S e-court page 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Just everyone is clear, Dr. Maric, Petko Cancar was -- had several official positions during the war. He was member of the Crisis Staff in Foca in 1992, he was deputy in the RS Assembly, and he was appointed advisor to the RS Presidency in July 1992. Can you confirm this, Dr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: He held many positions. I don't really know all of them, to be honest, but he had positions at the republican level before the war and after the war and also in the local community. And, by the way, he is a lawyer by occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is in D00440, page 3, and P03333, page 40. Dr. Maric, were you present in Foca for the town celebration of St. Nikola's day in 1994 during which officials of the RS leadership and religious heads were present? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember. I don't remember. But considering my profession, probably I was present if I was there, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let me show you a short video-clip of this event, and this is a speech made by Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the RS Assembly. I will be asking you to tell us whether you recognise the location and people present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter -- sorry, 65 ter 40254A, videotape V000-1078, time code 31 minutes, 4 seconds, 32 minutes, 52 seconds, date is 21 May 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Momcilo Krajisnik: Brothers and sisters, high priests, president of Srbinje Municipal Assembly, members of the Assembly, dear professor Kilibarda [phoen], dear people of Srbinje, it is a great pleasure to be among you after two and a half years. Today, unlike before, I see a true Serbian town. You proudly bear your true Serbian name. You are the example to all Serbs because you have managed to eliminate what was coming from this town. You prevented it so it would not happen. From this town, from this community, the hardest things were aimed at the Serbian people by the then-leaders of the Serbian ... um ... Muslim organisation, the organisation SDA. Mr. Izetbegovic then said that this town would be another Mecca. But you would not allow that. And for that, in the name of all Serbs, I thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Did you recognise this event, Dr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Momcilo Krajisnik who is standing on the pavement and giving a speech in front of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In Foca?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Did you recognise people present?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Well, I see some uniformed people. I didn't really pay attention and it doesn't really mean much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik said that Srbinje is a true Serbian town that proudly bears its Serbian name which, in fact, it was called Foca once before; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, the town was called Foca up until the decision of the Municipal Assembly by which the name of the town was changed to Srbinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Miroslav Stanic, member of the Crisis Staff in Foca, made statements on the Serbian television at Pale about the dedication of the Serbian commanders in Foca, as a result of which he said Foca is free without having a constant headache from the Mujezins singing from the top of the minarets. This was the reality of Foca, Dr. Maric. By the end of 1993 there was no mosques. There was no Mujezins in Foca; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: That was the policy I'm not familiar with. What I do know is that I received 352 dead at the morgue of the hospital. They were dead soldiers and civilians. And from the hospital morgue, as I was the manager during those years, they were all sent, 646 dead people from Foca. And as for the policies pursued by Miroslav Stanic, this is something I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I refer Your Honours to P03476, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic was in Foca in August 1993 and you received him there, and I believe you told us at the beginning about this event. Among the people present at the time there were Mr. Karadzic, Vojislav Maksimovic, Petko Cancar, Colonel Marko Kovac, and you, Dr. Maric. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: President Karadzic visited the hospital with his wife, Vojislav Maksimovic, professor and dean of the university, as in 1993 on the 15th of October in Foca. Thanks, among others, to the local and republican authorities, the medical and dental universities started working with enrolment of the first students and now it's been already 20 years that it's in operation. So this could have been the visit during which I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I asked you if these particular persons were present, do you recall, for example, Colonel Marko Kovac being there, commander of the tactical group Foca?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's see a transcript of the video of the radio broadcast of this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 24728A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see at line 21 of the previous page. Could you give the reference number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: My apologies. It's P03476, page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, in front of you there will be a transcript of the radio broadcast of the event that we are talking about. It starts with a report about the visit. It refers to you, among other people. And there is also a speech made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I believe we have it. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And it -- as you will be able to see, Dr. Maric, it starts with report about the visit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you see? I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought that we had it. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So -- and then there is a speech made by Mr. Karadzic which is on the second part of the page. Can we scroll down. He talks about Foca and about its future. At the bottom of the page and in next page Mr. Karadzic refers to the negotiations, and according to him the Muslim side does not ask for Zvornik or Foca anymore - can we also have next page - but for Visegrad and Bratunac which cannot be given. He said, and this is at second page: "It is important for the citizens of Foca to know that the Muslim republic gave up on Foca." Can we have last page, page number 3 in both languages. Mr. Maric the B/C/S should be on the screen, B/C/S. I would like to read this portion of the transcript and I would like you to confirm this -- that these were your words. Can you see it, Dr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the key so we could see who UM is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, I believe, just confirmed these were his words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I did not confirm the words. I'm reading the text which is presented to me. Please, please. Since January 1993 I was the acting director of the hospital in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: My apologies. I have to interrupt you. But if you read this portion, perhaps you can remember whether these were your words; and if not, so I can play you tape -- I can play the tape of this portion.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Well, look, it's been 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I understand. But if you read, perhaps you'll recall. And you recalled event at the beginning when I asked you about this event. It refers to the Serbian university --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we should see the video, then this would be no doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's an audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It is an audio, a radio broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can hear it so that the witness can see if he recognises his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So I need 65 ter 24728A, clip number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Unknown man: ... with the work for which we are motived. We have shown that we can continue and President Mr. Radovan Karadzic will continue to be happy with our work, as he approves our plans and encourages us in our sound medical views about the future and in general, both with respect to the clinical centre and the education facilities, to establish a Serbian university. The three faculties which it will comprise with a high quality will be the same level of quality as the one at Sarajevo university when it was set up in 1946. Again, this medical school must be the first faculty to open up in our new state."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, are you satisfied that these were your words?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And when I said "clip," the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps wait, Dr. Maric, I have limited time. Unless it is related to this clip, and if you can ask Chamber to allow you to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, did you want to add anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm asking to say that the university in the Serbian Sarajevo, the medical and dentistry school in Foca is part of the university in Serbian Sarajevo. That's all I wanted to add. On 15th of October we started working at the university as well, and these preparations started in 1992 so that there would be two university schools in a town that had never had a university before. My -- that was the thrust of my speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just clarify that we have this complete clip in evidence from the beginning when the reporter speaking, Dr. Karadzic's speech, and Dr. Maric's speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When I said we would admit it, I meant the pages we saw. But how many pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Three pages I believe, the complete thing, and we can provide those to all, just in case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any difficulty with it, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, let's talk about your colleagues, non-Serb doctors at the Foca hospital. You told us in paragraph 5 that they left the hospital and that no one drove them out. In fact, Dr. Maric, soon after the conflict in Foca started, non-Serb doctors and other non-Serb employees of the Foca hospital were either expelled or detained at KP Dom Foca, were they?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Are you saying that there was no non-Serb doctor detained at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Among the non-Serb doctors that were detained at the KP Dom were Dr. Amir Berberkic, Dr. Aziz Torlak, Dr. Ibrahim Karovic, medical technicians, Mato Ivancic, Izet Causevic, Zeco Mehmedspahic, Karabegovic, and others. Are you aware, Dr. Maric, that these people, your colleagues, were detained at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: My colleague Amir Berberkic was wounded. I operated on him on both of his knees. And after he was successfully treated, he left probably as a prisoner. He found himself in prison. Dr. Aziz Torlak was supposed to reunite with his family and with the medical convoy he left, and later I learned he was in the prison in Foca. My other colleagues were from the health centre. However, in early 1992 they had some problems at the health centre and they were probably transferred from the health centre because of those disagreements, I'm talking about Dr. Ibro Karovic, into the KP Dom. The medical technicians did not leave the hospital. They probably placed themselves at the disposal. Nobody was taken away from the building of the hospital. I say that with full responsibility except that Dr. Torlak left with a medical convoy towards Rogatica. They were in town not at the hospital, so they did not leave from the hospital and they were not taken away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence that Dr. Aziz Torlak was brought to the KP Dom from his work-place at the hospital; were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Dr. Torlak -- in fact Dr. Seku Stanic [phoen], director of the hospital --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It was a simple question. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: I cannot. I'm trying to tell you that Dr. Torlak was taken away with all the papers by a medical convoy. He was given an ambulance, too, to take him home. He was going to Rogatica, and then probably on the way from the hospital along those 2 kilometres this ambulance was stopped and Aziz was placed in the KP Dom, because I visited 15 days later to see what happened because he's my colleague, a surgeon. He was going home and he found himself in the KP Dom. I went with a colleague to the KP Dom to see what I can do because I'm a responsible person, a responsible work colleague, and that was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I refer to P03335, page 1212. Can we have now 65 ter 24767.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is an order issued by Colonel Marko Kovac, commander of the Tactical Group Foca. This order was issued pursuant to the order of the VRS Main Staff for the release and hand-over of Dr. Karovic to the representative of the exchange commission, Slobodan Mitrovic. Dr. Maric, your colleague, Dr. Karovic, was detained at the KP Dom; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: He's a colleague from the health centre, but that's true. He is a colleague from a different health institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6206, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's talk about the medical treatment at the KP Dom. Dr. Maric, the KP Dom detainees died as a result of lack of medical treatment. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No, and I don't believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence that KP Dom detainees Esad Hadzic, Omer Kunovac, and Ibrahim Sandal died as a result of sickness and beatings. Were you aware that this was happening at the KP Dom, Dr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: All the sick and seriously ill from the KP Dom were brought to us to the hospital. They were treated or operated on regardless of the fact that they were at the correctional penitentiary facility. It's impossible for a person to have died without having been to the hospital before. You should look at the documentation from the hospital and you would see that I operated on people from the prison. They came to get specialised treatment, but what was going on at the prison I don't know because I had no occasion to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer to P03568 page 2824 and P03335, page 1230 to 33 and page 1255.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, among the detainees at the KP Dom there were Asim Hadzimuratovic, Hamdija Hadzimuratovic, and Rasim Jusufovic, former patients of the Foca hospital who had heart surgery performed on them before the war. They did not receive treatment for their condition during the detention. Did you know this, Dr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I referred to P03335 page 1220 to 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has also received evidence that during the winter 1992/1993, the KP Dom detainees were held in the cells with no heating provided. The food and the hygienic conditions were poor. Some of the detainees had lost up to 40 kilos of their body weight by this point. Some got lice on their bodies. Were you aware of these conditions at the KP Dom, Dr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Health care for detainees in the prison is the responsibility of agencies outside the public health care fund or budget, so I was not aware of this. All they needed the hospital could have provided to them. My colleagues went to see those patients when their own doctors were absent. They came to the hospital to be seen. That's all I know. I've been to the KP Dom only once when I went there to see -- to visit my colleague, Dr. Aziz, to see what had happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer to P03335, page 1226 to 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence that a male nurse by the name of Gojko Jokanovic was the only medical personnel at the KP Dom and that Dr. Cedomir Dragovic visited the KP Dom. Dr. Dragovic was a gynaecologist, wasn't he, Dr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, his specialisation was gynaecology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I refer Your Honours to P03335, page 1266; and page [sic] 03349, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Amir Berberkic testified in the case of Milorad Krnojelac that Dr. Drago Dragovic and later Dr. Vladicic [phoen] came to the KP Dom once a week and that there was a queue during the visits. They only asked prisoners about their health in the presence of the guards without conducting any examination. This is at transcript page 23 -- sorry, 3740 to 41 of the Krnojelac case. Dr. Maric, this was how the medical treatments were conducted at the KP Dom. Did you know this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I cannot accept that a doctor would go there and conduct an examination in that way. That is contrary, it cannot fit in with our concept of medicine and the Hippocratic oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's talk about the log-books that you referred to in paragraphs 11, 12, 21 to 23 of your statement. It is my understanding that you provided copies of these log-books, did you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: The service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And then you took from the service and you provided to the Defence copies of these log-books that we talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: The service. No, that's the regular service that took only the documents because there are permanent records of the hospital and it can be obtained at the request of the proper agencies. I only approved it. It all came officially. I did not bring any documents, but I have the originals in the archives in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I take it it was you who decided which pages should be provided, did you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No, no. Well, we couldn't do that with protocols. We have protocols covering 1500 to 2.000 patients. The number admitted in 1992, we couldn't take all of that. We took only examples, samples to show you, for you to see that there were 268 non-Serb patients treated that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's first have a look at the log-book of the children's department, 1D07238.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to get through this material fast I have prepared charts for the log-books that Dr. Maric provided and I have hard copies of these charts and also they are uploaded in e-court as 65 ter 24796.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we get an explanation why there is no type of service indicated or no outcome of the treatment. Why is this selected in this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
