utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- we considered to include what is the issue before the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, if you look at the chart that you have in front of you of the children's department log-book, it shows that 15 Muslim children were received at the hospital in the period from 7 April 1992 to 3 December 1992. Dr. Maric, these children survived some of the most horrific events. They watched their parents being killed or expelled and they were left behind. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a reference to this? What kind of examination is this? How do we know this? Where is this information?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: These are my questions for the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is testifying. This is not a question. We don't have a reference for this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... coming up also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He is. He's doing his cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic. This is an improper intervention on your part. Please continue, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So did you know, Dr. Maric, what happened to these children?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. I'm a doctor at that hospital. What we see on the screen is the sequence of admission. This is a protocol of the paediatric department. Every ward has its own protocol, its own record of admission of patients into that ward. This is the sequence in which they were admitted and discharged with the result of having improved or been cured or transferred to a different health care institution. These are the categories we have in the medical profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While your time is up -- but let us be clear, what document are we looking at now? Are we looking at the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President. So this is -- on the screen is document 1D07238 and you should have chart -- the first page of the chart like an overview that's been prepared of this log-book. That's on the hard copy that I gave to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, also, I think Dr. Karadzic did have a good point. When you look at line 61 -- page 61, line 4, that -- whenever it's been put to the witness, that's a statement by the Prosecution. So then he -- when it came time to ask his question he just said: Do you know what happened to these children? But that was not the same question he was implying by his own intervention. So I think he should be required to put to the doctor whether or not the doctor knows that the children that are listed here survived and watched their parents being killed or expelled while they were left behind. Since the Prosecutor made that statement, he should be required to put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I will, Your Honours, in a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, did you know children by the name of Kemal Soro and Azra Ramovic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No, not by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Kemal is listed in item 160 of this log-book and it is at English page 18, B/C/S page 5, of the log-book. Kemal is also listed in the chart in front of you. We have his statement. Kemal said that one day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's do it one by one. So show the Kemal one from the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the B/C/S if you look at the last, last row you see it's one -- item number 160.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So make sure that e-court is following so that the witness can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, we have statement of Kemal. He said that one day Serb soldiers attacked his house in the area of Foca called Codor Mahala. His father and his uncle were taken to the KP Dom. Kemal moved to his grandparents' house about 2 kilometres away. His mother and brother stayed in Foca. The statement of Kemal is 65 ter 24774. We can have it on the screen, and I need page 4. Kemal said that the Serb soldiers attacked this area as well. They set the house on fire, and Kemal heard shots. He was hiding on a tree nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We would need page 4 of the statement, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Next morning everyone from the house was missing, Kemal's grandfather, uncle, two aunts, and their children. Kemal went to the house of Serb neighbour. The neighbour directed Kemal to the hospital. At the hospital Kemal was placed into a room with Muslim children only. There was a girl by the name of Azra.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you look at the chart Azra Ramovic is listed in the log-book twice at item numbers 153 and 182 at English pages 17 and 29, B/C/S pages 5 and 8. According to the log-book, Azra was 4 in 1992. Kemal said that Azra had injuries all over. Azra told Kemal that his mother and brother were killed at the house in Foca where she was. According to Azra, soldiers set the house on fire and shot those outside, the people that were in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, this is what was happening to these children. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: I don't have the protocols on the screen showing these children. I'm not a paediatrician, but I know the rules. Since the paediatric ward is small, and if they have been successfully treated but still remain in the hospital, then we placed them in departments where there is room. I had the Serbian version of the protocol. Now I see only the English one, but I could see that he, this boy, was moved to the ophthalmology department. I don't know anything about these events if you ask me about them. I'm a surgeon and for 30 days I did not leave the OR. I don't know the things that you want me to answer. That's the only fair thing I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, the Serb authorities considered these children for exchange, that is, to send them over to the other side in order to get a Serb back. Did you know this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we were the one to suggest first that children should be united with their families, but we did not succeed. Where we did succeed is that one boy, Djuderija, was exchanged for some of our people. But I don't really remember this exactly. It was the wish of the authorities of both sides, I suppose, because they knew about these children who remained in the hospital in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have P06080.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is a combat report sent by Colonel Marko Kovac to the Herzegovina Corps in October 1992. In item number 3 he refers to the visit of the ICRC to the hospital, and according to this report they talked to the Muslim children. At the end of the report Colonel Kovac refers to these children again, and he said: "If there is interest, we have 21 Muslim child and a number of women for exchange or we would send them to Gorazde." This is, Dr. Maric, how it was dealt with these children. Did you know this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No, no. I've already stated --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's have a look --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be allowed to have a say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What did you wanted to say, Mr. -- Dr. Maric? Did you want to say something in response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I don't want such statements made about patients regardless of their ethnicity at the hospital in Foca. We treated all patients the best we could under those circumstances, with the food we had, with the supplies we had. We did not treat them according to their ethnic background. I've never stated that. I've never said anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the log-book of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much more do you need, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I have prepared is I want to deal with the general admission log-book, there's a second log-book, and I had two newspaper articles about Foca today and the witness. So if you allow me, I would only cover the next log-book and I would finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems you do not pay any attention to the time-limit the Chamber has imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm trying my best, Mr. President, and we had problems with e-court and I'm trying -- and I apologise to cutting witness's answer. I'm doing my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue. I'm confident you can conclude before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I can stop whenever you wish me to. Can we have a look at admission log-book, that is 1D07239, and can we have it on the screen. And, Mr. President, I also prepared charts for this log-book that should be also in front of you like second document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us in paragraph 15 that the Serbian population was prevented from coming to the hospital during first days of the conflict because it was blocked by the Green Berets. Dr. Maric, the admission log-book that you provided shows that during this period there were patients of Serb ethnicity received at the hospital. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: The first wounded person of Serb ethnicity could have entered the Foca hospital on the 14th of April, 1992; that is Marijan Blagojevic. From the 8th until the 14th, not a single wounded Serb person could have reached the hospital. It was only civilians who were admitted into the hospital and there was no obstacle for civilians and ill persons. I already said that we had our first wounded person admitted on the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, if you look at the chart in front of you, that's the paper I provided earlier. Dr. Maric, it's hard copy. So if you take second document, that one, exactly. So if you look at that chart and that chart represents list of patients of Serb ethnicity that were received at the hospital in the period that we have in the log-book, that is from 7 April to 23 May. Please keep in mind, Dr. Maric, that each page of the B/C/S version of the log-book contains ten entries except for page 1 and 37 which have 11 entries. If you look at the chart, the column called B/C/S, you will be able to see that there were number of patients of Serb ethnicity received at the hospital during the first days of the conflict. For example, item numbers 2551 to 2670 at pages 1 to 12 of the B/C/S and 1 to 35 of the English cover period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So I'm referring to the log-book so -- and also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you take one by one. I can't follow this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So if you take that chart, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I received is just English showing the number of item -- the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Exactly, and that represents names of Serb ethnicity that were received at the hospital during the period we have in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So why don't we show the witness the correct column and rows.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: On the screen. Yes, we can do that. So it's 65 ter 24796.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the paper copies of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Rest assured they are just numbers. You can follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: 65 ter 24796. Second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, if you look the column B/C/S, each entry represents Serb patient received at the hospital and it covers all the entries from the beginning down to number 2667 represent Serb names. And this is the period from 7 to 17 April, which is ten days into the conflict. During these ten days there were about 40 patients of Serb ethnicity received at the hospital out of 121 entries for that period. So, Dr. Maric, patients of Serb ethnicity were received at the hospital during the first days of the conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, this list that we're given it doesn't include the names, so how is the doctor supposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he's putting his --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's hear the witness. Yes, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. I've said that wounded persons and injured persons could not enter the hospital in Foca until the 14th of April, 1992. Marijan Blagojevic was the first patient. Ill persons could probably be admitted because that was the only way in which it could be done. There was a war in Foca that went on for about eight days, fighting in town, and that was dangerous for all citizens. And what you see there in the protocol, those are ill persons. They came and that's why we admitted them. I've already said to the Defence, too, that we admitted wounded persons from Gorazde but we could not receive people from Foca because the road to the KP Dom across the Drina bridge, the iron bridge, was probably under some control and the forces would decide, probably, who they would let pass to the hospital. That is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Majority of the patients that asked for medical treatment at this first initial period were non-Serbs; however, by the end of April and in May the number of non-Serb patients drops and the number of Serb patients increases. If we look, for example, page 3 of the chart, these names listed there are also Serb -- patients of Serb ethnicity. And you can see every day -- like each page that you see B/C/S represents ten entries and as you can see every page contains majority of Serb patients that were received at the hospital. And this covers period late April/beginning of May. So were you aware that almost --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's stop here. You said names -- let me see. These names listed there are also -- where are these names appearing? You are saying that these numbers represent Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's the better --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- according to the original chart?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's the better way to put it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then you say B/C/S represents ten entries, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So every page in the B/C/S version of this log-book has ten entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is it clear from this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's your analysis?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Exactly. You would have to go back to the original log-book and you will be able to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then you may put the question to the Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Doctor, were you aware that almost by the end of May there were almost no non-Serb patients received at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Ill persons and wounded persons go to hospital, not Serbs and Muslims, first and foremost. Secondly, I said for 268 ill persons, if you will, patients, Muslims, ethnic Muslims, they were treated in 1992. They were admitted from April until September and discharged as they would be cured throughout 1992, except for those seven children who stayed behind and in 1993 we took them to Igalo. Certainly the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the war operations did have an effect in terms of where patients would decide where they thought that they could find the best medical treatment for them. So if you're just looking at the ethnic background and how sharp the decline was per month, well certainly people wouldn't want to go to hospital where they could get in trouble if it's, say, Serb-controlled territory. So I don't know about those patients and what the truth is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would offer these charts into evidence so you can look at them and compare against the original log-books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you want to say something, Dr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have documents that were photocopied. That's the only thing I can see. As for these tables, I accept them just because I'm sitting here but I cannot accept them as documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it this is a summary analysis from the original document. You can use it as your supplementary material when you make your submissions instead of tendering it as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's fair. I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will -- just -- I haven't heard from the Defence. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's my position also. It's a tool for argument, not a matter for evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, but I was involved in an earlier exchange where -- and Mr. Zec has been very polite about not referencing this, we tried to seek an agreement or an understanding or stipulation from the Defence about the original logs and the ethnicity of the names of the patients who appeared there, which seemed a pretty reasonable request when that's the focus of this submission by the Defence in the first place. But inexplicably they refused, which one could consider to be an effort to have us press up against the time allocations and Mr. Zec tried to deal with it as effectively as he could under the circumstances, but I noted that there was -- there seemed to be some implied criticism of Mr. Zec for trying to take this approach under the circumstances which would have been obviated with a little bit of comity, that is, with agreement from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, in order to admit this one, witness should have confirmed each item which is Serb or not. We didn't go through this document and the Defence is opposing. It's not in agreement, so what's the basis that we can admit it? We can use it as your submission --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand the Court. I wasn't arguing with the position the Court now feel forced to take, but I was suggesting that I think unreasonably, especially given the basis for which these logs were tendered, that the Defence refused to acknowledge what Mr. Zec was trying to point out and that if we had sufficient time could have been done directly with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the Chamber has the sympathy with the points raised by Mr. Tieger, but under the circumstances we'll not admit this. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yeah, so, Mr. President, just to make my point, perhaps we can show the last page of the log-book, that is, 1D07239 and you can follow also at the last page of the chart, there's page 39. And there are ten entries here at the chart, and I will ask the witness to go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's upload that one, Exhibit D3130. Let's switch to the e-court. I don't think there's an English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: There is no English. I don't believe that we have correct log-book in B/C/S. So I have 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we do. It's page 40 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we -- so is that page 40?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is the last page, and the exhibit was MFI'd for that reason that we don't have a full translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I understand because we asked the Defence to remove page 40 because it's unrelated, so we need page 39.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this page number 40, we tendered it as a separate document and it has been admitted as a separate document and its removal had been requested now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So now, Mr. President, this page, page 39 in B/C/S, contains entries from item number 2931 to 2940. And you can find it on the last page of the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Maric, Dr. Maric, can you read the names and tell us their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: I cannot. I cannot see this well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we perhaps if Doctor cannot --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: I can see -- well, I can read this. It's some page from the protocol. It starts with 2.931. I cannot see this first one Brod, Foca, Maglic, then Skipina, probably Pavlovic, Vukovic, then the eye department. The second column are the departments where they were admitted probably, probably the Loktic [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please try to read the names on the end and tell us whether they are Serbs or Muslims, if you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can go every page, but we have simply no time and I can conclude at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Excellencies, before the break, can I call up page 38 just one page before this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no. How much do you need for your re-examination, Mr. Karadzic? Is that the only question for you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, I would need some 10 or 15 minutes, but since it's fresh in our minds I would like to show how the Prosecution selectively chooses its pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well then please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 38, please, of this same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's -- we have no problem with the -- you showing the witness but your comment is improper.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not going to affect the witness. Please. This has to do with facts and facts are obstinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Maric, are all these people Serbs? And who is not a Serb, could you please give us the name of that person. This is the 21st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think you haven't got your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Number 2927, that's a Muslim, a Muslim woman, Mejra Murat [phoen].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll the page down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Only to note for the record that these two names, these two entries that Doctor just read are not in the chart as of Serb patients and so -- this page 38 contains only eight names out of ten and this is what we asked the Defence on Friday if we could agree on so this wouldn't be an issue at all in court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow. Eight names out of ten?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct. Because on page 38 Doctor just read two names as Muslim patients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how -- where do you have eight in your chart? Ah, yes, in -- it's last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, correct. Last page and you should follow this row 38. That's the page, 38, that we are just looking at. And Doctor read two names, two entries, 2927, 2929, as Muslim names and they are not in this chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without your explanation, it's very difficult to follow. Now I see the point. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Maric, to the best of your knowledge, on the 21st of May was a Muslim returned and were these -- when these two Muslims were admitted?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No. I repeat yet again, throughout 1992 Muslims were treated, patients of Muslim ethnicity were treated in the hospital in Foca and were then discharged. They were admitted until September. I do not see the records now for after September that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's time for the break then I'm going to continue with the rest after the break or should I continue now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 45 minutes. Before that -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Mr. President, I neglected to introduce our intern, Alice Yang, from Taiwan who's been with us during this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at 1.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.41 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce Pauline Wilson of Australia who is a legal intern with our team and will be joining us during this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please have, for example, in this -- the first page in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I please ask you to read out the names of the Muslims of the ten persons listed here, or you can say the numbers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please see the following page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you read out the name of -- under number 2561.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gogic, Ivanka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is he Serb or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging by the last name, yes, but judging by the first name, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If any of the assistance, in the translation page 1 it's Jovanka Gogic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you say for Gogic, are the Gogic's Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you once again just to read out the numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't go further into this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But just a second, could we also please have just one more page, please, the next one. If that was number 60 then it has to be more than that. Just a second, 60 -- it should begin with 2571. Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you also read out the names --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- again where the patients are ethnic Muslims and what these dates are. The 4th of July, that's up until when you kept the last one at hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 4th of July, 80 -- no, these are the days, not the year, 1997 but 87 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read out the numbers which referred to, I think, Muslim patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Dr. Maric, once again I wish to ask you the following: Did you ever, you or someone from your service, send back an ethnic Muslim or made any sort of difference in terms of treatment?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the statement. And if you can please help me, this statement of this little Kemal which was quoted. I would like to have that in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It is 65 ter 24774.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Mr. Zec. Can we please see that in e-court and I would need the last page, please. The one-but-last then, please, the penultimate page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As we only have this in English, I will now read this out to you. It says in third line from above: [In English] "I heard that she was later taken to a place where many women were raped ..." [Interpretation] And then it goes on. And this has to do with the hospital: [In English] "At the hospital, we were generally treated well. But there was one female doctor who used to beat up children. I do not recall her name. She was elderly, very thin, had black hair and wore glasses." [Interpretation] And generally speaking, how does this correspond with your impressions that they were generally treated well, and was there a thin doctor wearing glasses who was beating children?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could it have been somebody else who was a staff member?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did the patients get as food?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: In the beginning from the 8th of April, as at least 500 civilians had entered the hospital complex, the patients and the staff, we all shared whatever we had in our supplies at the hospital depot. And whatever was served to the patients was also the food provided to any staff who were in the hospital and the situation was like that for the first ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us this, on page 59 you were asked today and it was suggested to you that examinations were carried out by group. Can you tell me if there is some doctor's activity at a hospital where something is done with a group of patients, usually in the morning?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Well, not in a group, but these are visits, the rounds, where we as the doctors do the rounds of the hospital and see all individual patients. Then we analyse the information and this is the only thing I know about that is done as a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was described to you as a group examination, how would you fit that in the practice of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't fit it in. Perhaps these were some psychological tests, if some psychologists did some tests jointly and then you would have a group of people who are given one and the same task and they are trying to do it. Apart from that, I could not imagine a doctor examining a number of people at the same time. In view of our obligation with regard to the protection and protecting the intimacy of the patients, they cannot be allowed to look at one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe to the Trial Chamber how does the morning round look, where are the patients and where is the medical staff and the doctor's team?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: The chief of service leads the team of his doctors together with the nurses who are in charge of these patients. The patients are in the rooms in their beds waiting for the rounds, and the round lasts depending on the specific problems that have to be dealt with and the illnesses in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether all the Muslims the medical staff orderlies and doctors were arrested and taken to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: No. Rather, all of us together as there were few of us, both of us, the Serbs and the Muslims, the gynaecologist, were my assistant as I am a general surgeon and worked in all departments and sections and admitted the injured and the ill people because our capacities were small. Today, the university hospital had 100 specialist doctors and then there were barely 20 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What would then be the basis for several people who are mentioned here, Ibrahim Karovic, and, I don't know, a few others to be taken into custody? Was it on account of their religion, profession, or was it a third factor?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Probably, though I don't know and I cannot accept that it could have been profession because we were -- perhaps something that's equal to all people, perhaps something third, if there was something. If there wasn't, well, they would know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 57, or rather, 51 in line 10 of today's transcript, you were asked something and then the following question was whether you remembered and you said "no, no, no." Let me read that out to you. What does that refer to, this "no, no, no"? We have to clarify this. I apologise. Page 51, here it is, line 10. From line 7 the question is: [In English] If these particular persons were present, do you recall, for example, Colonel Marko Kovac being there, commander of the tactical group Foca?" Your answer is: "No, no, no, no." [Interpretation] Did you answer that Kovac was not present or was it an answer to this part of the question asking you whether you remember?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: I don't remember and this is why I said that. And I answered to that effect, no, no, because 20 years later I do not remember whether I met someone at a specific place or said something at a specific place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Some parts of the political discussion in the parliament were also quoted to you and specifically the words of Mr. Petko Cancar. I wanted to ask you something about the Mujezins. Was there some disagreement about the loud tone used in loud-speakers when they would play this and did this bother one or the other group?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, perhaps on the first two or three days, Radio Foca was abused and Semso Tucakovic, who was the director, abused it, and he informed us as the citizens that around 5- to 6.000 armed men were entering the town and threatening in particular the Muslim population, which caused panic among the people. It was easiest to find refuge with us at the hospital because we provided shelter to everyone and so many people - I don't know the exact number - but about 500 people or perhaps up to 800 people came to the hospital and stayed within the hospital complex at the beginning of the war, that is to say in early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 50 someone was quoted as saying what sort of messages were arriving from Foca and that it was supposed to be turned into another Mecca. Can you tell us whether you know what this was based on, what the deputy said about the messages from Foca? Had there been anything from the beginning of the multi-party system which could have been interpreted as a message coming from Foca?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: There was a big rally in Foca during the election campaign, so probably the great numbers of people who attended and who arrived in Foca from all around was a sign based on which someone could have drawn such a conclusion. In the archives of Foca town there are documents about the building of one of the centres which was supposed to be high educational institution that would be devoted only to one ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I know you said that you didn't study political issues, but as you were a deputy were you aware that there were ongoing negotiations about establishing two municipalities within Foca?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Well, we have two municipalities and that idea --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before you continue. Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This goes beyond cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm laying the groundwork for my question and the question is in reference to what Mr. Zec said, that there is not a single Muslim left in Foca. You should have a little faith in me. I'm not so inexperienced anymore. It's been three years. In fact, I've been sitting in the courtroom for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were told here that somebody had said there were no more Muslims in Foca. Is it the case there were no Muslims in Foca and did the Serbs control all of Foca?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: There is Foca Ustikolina and Foca proper, that's the Foca as it was before the war. Foca Ustikolina is populated by Muslims and the Serbs live in Foca, and that works well. We divided right at the beginning. So if you look at the entire municipality that Foca covered, had the same numbers of people as on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian Foca are there any Muslims? Were there any during the war?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Well, I said judging by my patients there were Muslims and judging by the number of patients there should be the corresponding number of families, at least the patients from Foca had families in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The witness said that there are Muslims to date in the Serbian part of Foca. Did you say that there are Muslims in Foca?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Maric, for coming to testify. Just one more question. You said that I supported you. Did anyone from the authorities reproach you for your unbiased treatment of Muslim civilians and Muslim injured and wounded?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: As a physician and later as the director of the hospital, I had an exceptionally good co-operation with the local authorities. I want to say it was not just lip service. In 1992 we were already preparing premises and apartments and we were finishing building for the university to start in Foca. And it is thanks to that and all our efforts despite the war that Foca today has over 2.000 students. As for the authorities, they never pressured me. As head of the hospital I had a misunderstanding with them at a point in time when the town did not have its own morgue and the army did not have a morgue, and they were using hospital premises. And when there were battles with big loss of life, such as the battle at Josanica, there were many dead, and the military authorities had no understanding for our limitation of our capacities. You have to receive the bodies, make all the records, et cetera, and they couldn't understand why we couldn't do it fast enough, meeting all their demands and requirements. That's what I have against the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the civilian authorities, myself and the minister of health, how did they view the fact that you did not distinguish between the Serb wounded and the Muslim wounded?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: With approval --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. President, whether we still again go beyond cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Mr. Zec. Unless you have further questions, please conclude. You almost said thank you to the Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do, Your Excellency. This featured also in cross-examination. There was the question of names and lists. I want to see where he ended up after treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you, what did the Serbs do with the captured Muslim wounded? Where did they bring them?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: They brought them to our hospital for treatment. They brought them to us. I said in my previous answers that all the prisoners, captives, if they needed to be treated, were treated at the hospital and kept there as long as they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And after treatment, where does such a patient go?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO MARIC
utterances.text: He would be discharged to the hospital or back to whoever brought them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So a captive would be treated and then discharged and returned. Thank you, Dr. Maric. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Maric. That concludes your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On behalf of this Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to the appeal by Milan Martic, we also would be making submissions. We didn't receive anything until this morning also, so I assume it's okay for us to make those by the close of business tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. Please be seated. Make yourself comfortable, please. Do you hear me in the language you understand, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Simic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of procedure and evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you, and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence except and save the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we speak at a moderate rate so that they may be recorded, and between my question and your answer let us make a short pause, that is to say wait for the cursor to stop. Did you, Mr. Simic, give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court 1D7930.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told that due to the upgrading of the e-court system, we are not at the moment able to see the document. But given that the witness has his statement with him, why don't we proceed with the hard copies if the Prosecution is not opposed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That should be fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, this turbo process works with technology from the previous century. We should do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at your statement and confirm that that is, indeed, the statement you have given us and tell us how you read it. Have you signed it?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC
utterances.text: This is the statement I brought with me, yes, I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that statement faithfully reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put to you the same questions in the courtroom today as my Defence team has before me, would they be the same?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would. But there is a small mistake. In point 16 of the corrigendum it's not "1992," it's "1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So point 16 should read "mid-November 1991"?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC
utterances.text: That's correct, not 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's now on record. Are there any more corrections?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the rest correspond to what you said?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC
utterances.text: There is one point that is not quite clear, but it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need a minute to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please take your time, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 39, the last paragraph, all were armed and in civilian clothing. The word "and" should not be there. It's suffices to delete the "i."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you, did I understand this correctly. All who were there were in civilians clothing and some of them only were armed, but even those armed wore civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, because currently you could understand that everybody was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The rest is exactly what you said?

utterances.speaker: CVIJETIN SIMIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
